title: High flow oxygen therapy with automatic closed-loop controlled oxygen titration in hypoxemic respiratory failure: a randomized-controlled trial.
summary:
Part of the lungs' functions is to supply the body with oxygen by enriching the blood and to exhale carbon dioxide. In the case of respiratory failure, gas exchange in the lungs is impaired, which can lead to an oxygen deficiency. This undersupply can be treated with externally supplied oxygen, e.g. via a nasal cannula. If the oxygen supply via a conventional nasal cannula is not sufficient, a higher oxygen flow can be administered via a special device, whereby the inhaled air is warmed and moistened via a tight-fitting nasal cannula. This therapy is called high-flow oxygen therapy. The higher oxygen flow supports breathing and reduces the work of breathing. The supply of oxygen to the body is assessed via oxygen saturation, among other things. This is measured with a clip on the finger, toe or ear using a pulse oximeter. Based on the measured oxygen saturation, high-flow oxygen therapy has so far been set manually by nurses or doctors. New ventilators can measure oxygen saturation using a connected pulse oximeter and use these values to automatically adjust the settings for high-flow oxygen therapy. Target values and ranges are defined and set in advance by doctors.
Among other things, the automated setting can reduce the time in which the blood is saturated and supplied with too little oxygen. The aim of our research project is to investigate this.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Patients with hypoxemic respiratory failure admitted to IMC ward 37-4 or ICU 32-3
- Need for HFOT with ≥ 40 L/min with a FiO2 ≥ 0.30
- HFOT foreseeable on admission for at least 24 hours
Exclusion criteria:
- Age ≤ 18 years
- Pregnancy
- Expected or present dyshemoglobinemia
- Poor signal quality of SpO2 measurement at finger and ear (quality index < 60%)
- Haemodynamic instability (noradrenaline or adrenaline with a necessary continuous infusion of > 1 mg/h)
- Severe respiratory acidosis with pH < 7.25
- Difference between SpO2 and SaO2 of more than 5%
